newsitem.title: UK: IRA kills two policemen in Northern Ireland.
newsitem.headline: IRA kills two policemen in Northern Ireland.

text.p: Irish Republican Army guerrillas killed two Northern Ireland policemen in an ambush in the town of Lurgan on Monday, throwing the halting peace process into turmoil.

The officers were on routine patrol near the centre of the busy town in County Armagh when gunmen shot them at close range in the first IRA killing of policemen in the territory since it called off a ceasefire last year.
A caller using an IRA code word rang a Belfast radio station and said that that its "North Armagh Brigade" had "carried out this morning's attack".
A spokesman for British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who was attending a European Union summit in Amsterdam, said Blair was "appalled by this wicked and evil act" and awaiting further reports.

In a statement issued before the IRA's announcement, British Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam said that "At a time when Northern Ireland is holding its breath and hope for peace, those intent on evil have struck".
"The government resolutely condemns this atrocity but we will not be intimidated into weakening our resolution to bring about a peaceful Northern Ireland in which all can share."
Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn said the killings were "a very serious setback in the context of what politicians are trying to achieve in Northern Ireland".
The province has been tense ever since the IRA, which is fighting to end British rule, abandoned a ceasefire last year.
Mainstream Irish nationalist and Protestant unionist parties said the ambush was intended to increase divisions during an annual volatile period of street parades by Protestant groups.
They appealed to pro-British Loyalist guerrillas, who have maintained a shaky truce since October 1994, not to strike back and worsen the province's difficulties.
Loyalists have killed two people in the past year and set off sporadic bombs aimed at republicans, apparently in retaliation for republican hostilities.
Mowlam added that it was "vital that nobody takes the law into their own hands and that there is no retaliation in any shape or form".
Protestant politicians said Mowlam should abandon contacts with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, which London recently re-established in a bid to revive peace hopes.

"I don't think that there is any way that the government can continue with meetings with Sinn Fein/IRA while our policemen are being killed by the IRA or their friends," Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, told BBC radio.

Seamus Mallon, deputy leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, condemned the killings and said they were "designed to increase tension and to prevent a peaceful resolution of the marching problems".
The IRA seriously wounded a policewoman in a sniper attack in the city of Londonderry in April. Last week IRA members fired on a British army vehicle in the city but no one was hurt.
